name: Jackson Pr. 16.3: orbits circularize
description: Jackson Problem 16.3: an electron on an elliptic orbit radiates most near the nucleus, and its orbit becomes rounder as it decays. Two electrons with the same energy, one circling, one on an ellipse: the ellipse swings close to the nucleus early, but too fast to count. Bring both into the detector slowed by their radiation, in time.

reality.represents: Elliptic orbits round off as they radiate (Jackson Pr. 16.3)

remarks.detail: The electron radiates as Larmor's formula says and loses that energy through the Landau–Lifshitz force, exact in classical electrodynamics while the reaction is small against the Coulomb force.
An elliptic orbit radiates most near the nucleus, which takes away more energy than angular momentum there: the orbit becomes rounder as it decays.

remarks.line: A collapse within a few turns
remarks.detail: The atom is scaled so that it radiates away its orbit in a few turns (c = 2 cells per time unit); a classical hydrogen atom would circle about a hundred thousand times before collapsing, in about 10⁻¹¹ s. The nucleus is held fixed.

Real atoms do not collapse: quantum mechanics keeps the electron in stationary states, and it radiates only when it jumps between them. This classical collapse is the failure that made quantum theory necessary.
